chunks: Running tests 24/7 through outages. The question: Often times you need to run tests for days, weeks, or months continuously.
How do you ensure these tests run smoothly 24/7 for the entire time? What can you do to protect against power outages?
A test that runs for weeks must survive power cuts, crashes and full disks, or all the data may be lost.

The answer is layers: backup power to ride through short outages, automatic recovery so the setup restarts by itself and resumes where it stopped, and monitoring so a human learns fast if something fails.
A hospital cannot go dark. It has a battery system for the first moments, a generator for long outages, and staff who know the restart steps.
It also has alarms so someone notices a failure at 3 a. m. A 24/7 test setup needs the same layers. One difference: a test may be allowed to pause, as long as the gap is recorded.
The power path and the monitoring path. Everything the test needs sits behind the UPS, with a switched PDU so a single stuck instrument can be power-cycled remotely.
The generator and ATS extend the ride-through time beyond the battery.
UPS: uninterruptible power supply, a battery plus an inverter (which turns battery power into mains-style AC) that bridges short outages. Its energy is limited.
Graceful shutdown: saving work and closing the computer cleanly before the battery runs out. Checkpoint: saved test progress, so a restart resumes instead of starting over.
Heartbeat / watchdog: a regular "I'm alive" signal, and a timer that restarts the system if it stops.
A small UPS has two 12 volts, 9 Ah batteries (9 amp-hours: 9 amps for one hour), so 2 times 12 times 9 equals 216 watt hours.
With 85% inverter efficiency and 80% usable charge, a 300 watts load gets 216 times 0. 85 times 0. 8 over 300 about 0. 49 h, about 29 minutes.
That covers short outages and a clean shutdown. For an 8 hour outage at 300 watts you would need 2400 watt hours delivered, from a battery over 3500 watt hours.
So long outages need a generator, or a controlled shutdown plus automatic restart.
After power returns, the computer should power on by itself, start the test, read its checkpoint, and log the gap. An alert should go out. That is the whole idea.
"I'd layer it.
A UPS, ideally online, on the PC and instruments sized by load: about 29 minutes for 300 watts from a small battery, which covers short outages and a graceful shutdown.
A generator with an automatic transfer switch for long ones.
Then make it self-recovering: power-on-after-AC-loss, a test script that checkpoints its state and logs atomically, and a watchdog.
Add remote monitoring and alerts, plus checks on disk, temperature and cooling, and record any gaps in the data."
